content: In the early 1990s, Mexico demonstrated clear evidence of entering a transitional phase in the health status of its population. When compared to the conditions in 1940 or even 1970, mortality patterns in Mexico during the 1990s more closely resembled those observed in developed nations. Overall, the quality of health care in Mexico is excellent, and in many areas, it is exceptionally good. Most health care professionals in Mexico, including physicians and dentists, receive their training in Western countries such as the United States. Conversely, some American doctors also undergo training in Mexico, particularly in cities like Guadalajara. Medium-sized and large cities in Mexico typically have at least one high-quality hospital. A notable advantage of health care in Mexico is its affordability, with costs generally being significantly lower than those in the United States. This cost advantage extends to prescription medications, with drugs manufactured in Mexico costing, on average, about 50% less than their counterparts produced in the United States. During the Spanish conquest, the introduction of new diseases to the indigenous population led to widespread epidemics. Over the centuries, diseases such as smallpox, cholera, typhus, and measles caused significant mortality. In more recent times, urbanization and advancements in transportation have influenced the emergence of health epidemics. Socioeconomic disparities between the upper and lower classes have become increasingly evident in the health outcomes of the Mexican population. On one end of the spectrum, obesity has become a concern, while on the other, malnutrition and starvation persist, exacerbated by economic stagnation and financial crises. Certain health risks are more prevalent in Mexico due to cultural and lifestyle factors. For instance, the use of pesticides has become a significant health issue, particularly in states like Chiapas, where 58% of the population is engaged in agricultural work. Cultural attitudes play a critical role in shaping perceptions of health risks and the responses to them. Another pressing health concern in Mexico is the AIDS epidemic (referred to as SIDA in Spanish). In 1988, AIDS was the 11th leading cause of death in Mexico, but by 1996, it had risen to become the third leading cause of mortality, accounting for 12% of all deaths in the country. Advancements in medical science and increased health awareness have contributed to a 25-year increase in life expectancy during the latter half of the 20th century. While the health of the Mexican population has improved over the past four generations, millions of citizens still lack regular access to health care services. The health care system in Mexico is structured into three main components: Governmental health services include free care in rural areas provided by the Secretariat of Health, as well as family planning, vaccinations, oral rehydration therapy, and emergency services available nationwide at no cost. Between 1985 and 1995, the number of public hospitals in Mexico increased by 41%. In addition to public hospitals, private hospitals exist, but they require payment and often struggle to provide adequate care. Most private hospitals are small, with 83% of facilities having fewer than 14 beds, and half of those having fewer than 5 beds. Despite the expansion of public hospitals and alternative health services, approximately 11% of Mexico's population lacks access to health care in some form. Financial barriers are a significant factor, as the cost of medications and treatments can be prohibitively high. Many individuals are unable to take time off work to seek medical care, as even a single day of lost income can jeopardize a household's financial stability. Geographic barriers also exist, particularly in rural areas where residents may live far from urban centers and lack reliable transportation. Organizational barriers, such as mistrust in the health care system or concerns about the quality of services, further hinder access to care. These barriers often result in unmet medical needs, particularly in areas such as prenatal care, childbirth, acute illnesses, and injuries. For some families, medical costs consume more than one-third of their income. The health care system requires structural reforms to address the needs of a divided population and to improve access to services for the lower-income majority. Socioeconomic disparities also contribute to health inequities, particularly among indigenous communities. For example, 40% of indigenous women are anemic, compared to the national average of 26%. In low-income areas, fewer than 10% of pregnant women deliver their babies in hospitals. To address these disparities, the health care system must be restructured to reduce the divide between the upper and lower classes and to provide equitable access to care for all segments of the population.
